sweep_summary: Nyaturu (nyat1246) is not in the catalog. The single sweep item, Philippson 1991 'Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique orientale', was already on file (open author's PDF from DDL Lyon, fetched sources by the gwen1239 audit) and was copied to (+.txt) and logged in there. It treats Remi (F 32) at length (pp. 127-131, 392-393, 426-427, 433, 476, 485, 488, annex p. 503), on second-hand data from Olson 1964 and Schadeberg 1978/1978-79: Remi is 'strictement une langue à accent' in Philippson's sense (one lexically marked syllable per word, realised as a H on the following syllable; final marks retract to the penult in the word stratum; three disyllabic nominal schemes), with no length/intensity/pitch culmination on the penult and no demarcative stress. This is a restricted-tone/pitch-accent characterisation, not a fixed word-stress position; it agrees with Olson 1964 (tone language; stress only in Swahili loans), the best first-hand source, whose full text remains IA-lending/Harvard-print only. Nothing new to acquire from this item;g. Schadeberg 1978, Afrika und Übersee) were sought.

new_statements.translation_language: English (IA OCR; 'R^rai/Rqmi' normalised to R[į]mi, 'mpaaqga' to mpaaŋga)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Olson describes Rimi as a two-tone language (H vs L on every vowel, plus 1-3-mora vowel length); tone is the only suprasegmental phoneme he sets up. He attributes stress only to Swahili: in loans the Swahili penultimate stress is re-encoded as a long penultimate vowel whose first mora is High (falling HL), and long vowels also occur in the penult of many native verbs (1.10.3.6) -- but no stress or accent position is stated for Rimi words, and searches of the whole thesis for stress(ed)/accent(uation)/prominence/intonation/pitch/rhythm return nothing else. Olson 1980: 127 (saved, open) restates first-hand that Rimi 'is a tone language. It has only two tonemes'.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the loanword adaptation (Swahili penultimate stress > Rimi long HL penult) and utterance-final loss of a final High tone (Olson 1980: 128); pre-NC vowels lengthened to about 1.5 morae, 'not semantically significant' (1.10).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonemic inventory (suprasegmental phonemes per vowel); tone classes of nouns are said to be determinable only in context, not in isolation. No phrase-level stress/intonation statement seen. Caveat: read from search snippets, not full pages -- a sentence on non-phonemic stress elsewhere on p.29 cannot be fully excluded, though 'stress' itself occurs on no other page of the indexed scanned.
new_statements.identity_note: Olson 1964 is explicitly 'based on the Qirwana dialect' = Girwana (Glottolog girw1238, a dialect of nyat1246); Olson spells the language Rįmi (self-name Kirimi; people Arimi/Wanyaturu). Yukawa 1989's consultant is from Isuna village, Singida District (dialect not named). All sources refer to the same language, ISO rim.

new_statements.quote: On peut constater que le H apparaît régulièrement sur la syllabe suivant immédiatement celle qu'il caractérise dans la forme de base. Or, le remi peut être défini comme une langue accentuelle. Tous ses nominaux dissyllabiques se répartissent en trois schèmes seulement : I) NOmbE... "bovin" II) mbor&K... "chèvre" III) mp&oma... "babouin" [...] Il est d'ailleurs aisé de constater qu'il existe en remi une règle, d'application très générale, qui convertit tout schème -cvc*v en -c*vcv. [p. 485:] + remi : une marque finale se déplace sur la pénultième au cours de la strate du mot
new_statements.translation: One can see that the H regularly appears on the syllable immediately following the one it characterises in the base form. Now, Remi can be defined as an accentual language. All its disyllabic nominals fall into only three schemes: I) NOmbE 'bovine' II) mborí 'goat' III) mpóma 'baboon' [...] It is moreover easy to see that there is in Remi a rule of very general application which converts any -cvcv* scheme into -c*vcv. [p. 485:] + remi: a final mark moves onto the penultimate during the word stratum
new_statements.citation: Philippson, Gérard. 1991. Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique Orientale: étude comparative typologique et diachronique. Thèse de Doctorat d'Etat, Université Paris V. 542 pp. (NNT 1992PA05H011)
new_statements.locator: Ch. 4 sec. 4.1, p. 128 (with p. 485 sec. 3.5.2 d-II and Annexe p. 503)
new_statements.reading: Philippson's 'accent' is a lexically marked syllable realised by H tone (restricted tone / pitch accent), at most one per word; it is not stress. Rimi/Nyaturu has three lexical accent classes for disyllabic stems, the H surfaces on the syllable after the marked one, and a mark on a word-final syllable is retracted to the penult at the word level. The penult has no length, intensity or pitch culmination (Remi is absent from lists a-c of sec. 3.5.2, pp. 483-484) and no demarcative accent is recorded in the annex card (p. 503). Hence: no fixed-position word stress; a lexical tone/pitch-accent language. Analysis is second-hand (Olson 1964; Schadeberg 1978, 1978/79 — p. 520), not from the author's own fieldwork (p. 515). Consistent with Olson 1964 (tone language, 'stress' only in Swahili loans) already on file.
